turns.zh: 来认识一下 Emma。哎哟。她想 DIY 一个冬日仙境，却被金属丝缠住了。等等，那纸浆雕塑里是猫毛吗？

turns.en: I don't even have a cat.

turns.zh: 我们都有自己的长处，Emma。也许你的长处就是下载 Instacart 来订购节日装饰品。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.zh: 呃，Emma，你需要帮忙从金属丝里出来吗？

turns.en: We're not going to be able to make everybody happy if we talk too much about taking extra care for safety. People are going to accuse us of trying to slow down innovation. If we only talk about, "Hey, every it's got to be like max pedal to the metal." People will say, "Well, please don't kill us all."
turns.zh: 如果我们过多谈论格外注重安全，就无法让所有人满意。人们会指责我们试图减缓创新。如果我们只谈论“嘿，一切都得全速前进”，人们会说：“好吧，请别把我们全杀了。”

turns.en: This is Andrew Ross Sorkin with the New York Times and you're listening to interviews from our annual Dealbook Summit recorded on November 18th in New York City. Sam Altman and Greg Brockman founded OpenAI 11 years ago, next month as it happened. Sam is the chief executive. Greg is the president. Almost 4 years ago on November 22nd, 2022, they released ChatGPT built on a model called ChatGPT 3.5 and changed the world and we've been talking about it basically ever since. More than a billion people, I think it's a little over a billion two now are using ChatGPT every single week. And we've got about a million questions about the future and everything that's going on around us, as well as issues about security and safety and the economics of the new frontier, the politics of all of this. So, please welcome Sam and Greg together. Great to see you both. Thank you.
turns.zh: 我是《纽约时报》的 Andrew Ross Sorkin，您正在收听我们年度 Dealbook 峰会的采访，录制于 11 月 18 日的纽约市。Sam Altman 和 Greg Brockman 在 11 年前的下个月创立了 OpenAI，恰逢其时。Sam 是首席执行官，Greg 是总裁。大约四年前的 2022 年 11 月 22 日，他们发布了基于名为 ChatGPT 3.5 的模型构建的 ChatGPT，改变了世界，我们基本上一直在谈论它。超过十亿人，我想现在略高于 12 亿，每周都在使用 ChatGPT。我们有大约一百万个关于未来以及我们周围发生的一切的问题，还有关于安全和保障、新前沿的经济学以及所有这一切的政治问题。所以，请欢迎 Sam 和 Greg 一起上台。很高兴见到你们两位。谢谢。

turns.en: Thanks for having us.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请我们。

turns.en: There's about a million things to talk about. We have Anthropic's IPO happening tomorrow. We have the Jensen news. You have a new model that just came out yesterday. There's now security concerns. JD Vance is saying back in Washington, I think in part because of some of these things and I want to get to all of that. I know you've been asked about the Jensen situation and we were just talking about it backstage, but what do you think? I mean, you've watched this play out. Do you have a— I mean, what I'm curious, have you talked to him about this?
turns.zh: 有大约一百万件事要谈。Anthropic 的 IPO 明天就要进行。我们有 Jensen 的新闻。你们昨天刚发布了一个新模型。现在有安全担忧。JD Vance 在华盛顿发表言论，我认为部分原因是其中一些事情，我想谈到所有这些。我知道你们被问过 Jensen 的情况，我们刚才在后台也谈过，但你们怎么看？我是说，你们看着这件事发展。你们有没有——我好奇的是，你们和他谈过这件事吗？

turns.en: Do you want to go?
turns.zh: 你想先说吗？

turns.en: Either of you.
turns.zh: 你们谁都行。

turns.en: Look, I would say Jensen is singular. No question. And I have talked to him a little bit. My wife and I are friends with him and his family. And so, we just reached out personally just to be there for him and his family at this time.
turns.zh: 看，我会说 Jensen 是独一无二的。毫无疑问。我跟他谈过一点。我妻子和他及其家人是朋友。所以我们只是私下联系，在这个时刻陪伴他和他的家人。

turns.en: And how's he doing?
turns.zh: 他怎么样？

turns.en: Look, it was a personal private conversation is what I'd say. I think it's obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company. I think that what has been built there, what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last. And so, we're excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.
turns.zh: 看，我会说这是一次私人谈话。我认为这显然对每个人来说都是艰难时期，但再次，我认为 Nvidia 是一家如此了不起的公司。我认为那里建立的东西，Jensen 在那里建立的东西，显然是为了长久。所以我们很兴奋继续合作并展望未来。

turns.en: Sam, you speak to him, too?
turns.zh: Sam，你也跟他谈过吗？

turns.en: I did.
turns.zh: 我谈过。

turns.en: And?
turns.zh: 然后呢？

turns.en: Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia. It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen. I think singular is a great way to describe it. And
turns.zh: Jensen 最早对我们下了大赌注。我们对 Nvidia 也下了大赌注。很难想象没有 Jensen 的 AI 行业。我认为“独一无二”是一个很好的描述方式。而且

turns.en: Do you think he thinks he could come back?
turns.zh: 你觉得他认为自己能回来吗？

turns.en: Greg and I have like a little more empathy towards the situation than the average person. And I will say one thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory here or there. So I will say I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don't think the world needs another set of random opinions on what's going to happen here.
turns.zh: Greg 和我对这种情况比普通人更有同理心。我要说一件我不欣赏的事是地球上的每个人都在用这样或那样的随机理论猜测。所以我要说，我祝愿 Jensen 一切顺利。我祝愿 Nvidia 一切顺利。我不认为世界需要另一组关于这里会发生什么的随机意见。

turns.en: Let me ask you a philosophical question unrelated to Jensen but related in a way because I think about it a lot. I think about it in the context of this event actually. The idea of the cult of CEO so many of the people that are on this stage including both of you there is a cult of the CEO around them. The idea that some of these companies are so singular and these individuals are so singular and that they can't be run without them. You were pushed out and then came back in part because there was a view that certain people thought that you were both pushed out and came back. I don't like again all these differences between the situations tempting to put too much there. But I think a large part of what made OpenAI has made OpenAI succeed is that Greg and I have a unique partnership and brought something important to OpenAI. And did that over a period of now almost 11 years. Now could the company succeed without us? Yes. But do we together bring something that I think is important to what has driven OpenAI to where it is now? Absolutely. And I think that that has been our partnership together has been one of the most enjoyable parts of this for me over the last 11 years. I remember Greg early on in OpenAI would send me these screenshots and I think he even posted a few on Twitter of like how many hours a week he coded and it was this sort of like legend inside of OpenAI. Now Greg is operating in a different way and managing a company with that same ferocity and that is a special thing and I don't want to think about what OpenAI would be like without that. So is it true that I think people overproject onto any single person their importance to the company yes probably. Do I also think there are people and I'm very grateful to have gotten to work with Greg for so long as one of these people that do bring something that is very special and very hard to find also. Yes.
turns.zh: 让我问一个与 Jensen 无关但某种程度上相关的哲学问题，因为我经常思考它。实际上我是在这个活动的背景下思考的。CEO 崇拜的想法，这个舞台上很多人包括你们两位，周围都有 CEO 崇拜。认为其中一些公司如此独特，这些个人如此独特，没有他们公司就无法运营。你曾被赶出去然后又回来，部分原因是有人认为你们俩都被赶出去又回来了。我不喜欢再次，这些情况之间的所有差异，诱使人们过度解读。但我认为 OpenAI 成功的一大部分原因是 Greg 和我有一种独特的合作关系，并为 OpenAI 带来了一些重要的东西。而且这样做已经将近 11 年了。现在公司没有我们能成功吗？是的。但我们在一起是否带来了我认为对推动 OpenAI 走到今天很重要的东西？绝对是的。我认为我们的合作是我过去 11 年中最愉快的部分之一。我记得早期在 OpenAI，Greg 会给我发这些截图，我想他甚至在 Twitter 上发过一些，比如他每周编码多少小时，这在 OpenAI 内部成了传奇。现在 Greg 以不同的方式运作，以同样的凶猛管理公司，这是一件特别的事情，我不想想没有这个 OpenAI 会是什么样子。所以，我认为人们过度投射任何单个人对公司的重要性，这是真的吗？是的，可能。我是否也认为有些人——我非常感激能跟 Greg 合作这么久，作为这些人之一，确实带来了非常特别且非常难以找到的东西。是的。

turns.en: Can you just explain because I don't think we've actually seen both of you together on a stage like this before. You have historically been the face of this company and increasingly Greg you were sort of in the shadow I think but now increasingly are running the business. How do you guys work together? What is this partnership like? And longer term do you want to get into the shadow and him take the stage or how does this how's this going to work?
turns.zh: 你能解释一下吗，因为我认为我们实际上从未在这样的舞台上看到你们俩一起。历史上你一直是这家公司的门面，而 Greg 你越来越——我想你之前有点在阴影中，但现在越来越多地经营业务。你们如何合作？这种合作关系是什么样的？长期来看，你想进入阴影而让他上台，还是这如何运作？

turns.en: Do you want to go first and I'll take a second?
turns.zh: 你想先说，我接着说？

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: I mean, to understand how we work, I guess I would rewind to the very beginning of OpenAI. We did this dinner that Sam put together in July 2015, where we were talking about the idea that became OpenAI. Was it too late to start a lab with a bunch of the best people to really try to make a positive impact on AGI? And no one could come up with a reason it was sufficiently impossible. So Sam and I, driving back to the city together, looked at each other and were like, we have to do this. And I was between jobs at the time, so the next day I was full-time on it. Sam had a day job, but we were constantly on the phone with each other, probably like five, six times a day. We would call each other for two minutes at a time, just incredibly rapid fire. Just like the highest bandwidth interactions I've had in a professional setting with anyone. That's 100% how we started, how we operate today. And so probably over the past week, we've probably been on—I can't even count—a dozen, two dozen different topics we've been talking about. Sometimes together with other people, sometimes just us one-on-one, sometimes turning through pretty deep issues for longer calls, sometimes incredibly quick. And I think that bandwidth, that trust that we've built and the division of how we think about the different areas of responsibility—I think all of that is something we've really built up over these 11 years.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，要理解我们如何工作，我想回到 OpenAI 的最开始。2015 年 7 月，Sam 组织了一次晚餐，我们讨论了后来成为 OpenAI 的想法：现在是否已经太晚，无法聚集一批最优秀的人来真正对 AGI 产生积极影响？没有人能提出一个理由说明这足够不可能。所以 Sam 和我一起开车回城时，互相看着对方，觉得我们必须做这件事。我当时处于两份工作之间，所以第二天我就全职投入了。Sam 有日常工作，但我们经常通电话，大概每天五六次。我们每次通话两分钟，非常快速。这就像我在职业环境中与人进行的最高带宽的互动。100% 这就是我们开始的方式，也是我们今天运作的方式。所以大概在过去一周里，我们可能已经——我数不清——讨论了一二十个不同的话题。有时和其他人一起，有时只有我们一对一，有时为了深入的问题打更长的电话，有时非常快速。我认为那种带宽、我们建立的信任，以及我们对不同责任领域的划分方式——我认为所有这些都是在过去 11 年里真正建立起来的。

turns.en: What do you guys disagree about?
turns.zh: 你们在哪些方面有分歧？

turns.en: Well, I think the kind of thing that we tend to spend a lot of time on is really thinking about—I mean, to some extent, the thorniest questions in AI. Like, how do we think about what we're building? Where's the future going? How is what we did in the past not going to work for what we're doing going forward? How do we need to evolve it? How do we message it? How do we talk about it? How do we communicate it to the company? How do we execute? And so I think that we spend a lot of time going back and forth. Sometimes it's individual word choices. Sometimes it's like, should we really go into this area? But I think that we always come to—and sometimes it takes months, right, to come to convergence. But I think that there are times where we disagree and commit, and sometimes where we really grind it out and really come to a shared view.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为我们倾向于花大量时间真正思考——在某种程度上，AI 中最棘手的问题。比如，我们如何看待我们正在构建的东西？未来走向何方？我们过去所做的如何不再适用于我们未来要做的事情？我们需要如何发展它？我们如何传达它？我们如何谈论它？我们如何向公司沟通？我们如何执行？所以我认为我们花了很多时间来回讨论。有时是单个词的选择。有时是像我们是否真的应该进入这个领域。但我认为我们总是会达到——有时需要几个月才能达成共识。但我认为有时我们会保留分歧并承诺执行，有时我们会真正磨下去，真正达成共同观点。

turns.en: What do you disagree with them about? What do you actually disagree with about?
turns.zh: 你对他们有什么不同意见？你实际上在哪些方面有分歧？

turns.en: Yeah, I was going to say something similar. I think we could point to areas where we're like, we disagree about whether we should go after this new area or whether we should be focused a little more or focused a little less. But I think the most important areas are where we disagree and then come together in some way in the middle. So if there—and some of these like most important questions now about—there's been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future. And there's increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And we both agree that that's a terrible idea. But the question of how to actually prevent that from happening, how to actually ensure that we will—given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do—that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way and we don't have this either accidental or intentional handover. I think we can both agree on that. We'll both have a little bit of a different view of what does it actually take to get there and what are the landmines along the way, how do we actually ensure it. And that's where I think us debating and really grinding down the—
turns.zh: 是的，我想说类似的话。我认为我们可以指出一些领域，比如我们是否应该进入这个新领域，或者我们应该更专注一点还是不那么专注。但我认为最重要的领域是我们有分歧，然后以某种方式在中间达成一致。所以如果有一些——现在一些最重要的问题关于——硅谷一直有这种几乎荒谬到需要抗争的事情，但我们都深信人们需要保持对未来的控制。越来越多的人谈论说，要么将会，要么应该有这种逐渐移交给 AI 的过程。我们都同意那是个糟糕的主意。但问题是如何真正防止这种情况发生，如何真正确保我们——考虑到各种压力和其他公司可能尝试做的事情——我们将真正确保人们以非常深入的方式保持对未来的控制，我们不会发生这种意外或故意的移交。我想我们都同意这一点。我们对于实际需要什么才能达到那里、沿途有哪些地雷、我们如何真正确保它，会有一些不同的看法。这就是我认为我们辩论并真正磨下去的地方——

turns.en: I want to dig in on this because this is a very, very important issue about this idea of humans in the loop. I always thought—
turns.zh: 我想深入探讨这个问题，因为这是一个非常非常重要的问题，关于人类在环中的想法。我一直认为——

turns.en: Not in the loop, in control.
turns.zh: 不是人在环中，而是人在控制。

turns.en: In control. Okay. Um, but we are now in a moment and it goes to some of the issues we're seeing around the country right now, but we're in a moment where people are worried that AI is taking over and doing things on its own. And I always thought the idea was that AI was for it to work, it was supposed to do things on its own. Uh we're going to talk to Satya Nadella later today and he came out about a month ago and he said he believes that this idea of alignment—that the models themselves can never actually be aligned. They can't be aligned with what humans want. That the only sort of answer to this is to contain them. Meaning that the AI will always just do whatever it's going to do and that you need to then create sort of container systems and police on top of them. If that's true, does any of this even make sense?
turns.zh: 在控制。好的。嗯，但我们现在处于一个时刻，这涉及到我们目前在全国看到的一些问题，但我们处于一个人们担心 AI 正在接管并自行做事的时刻。我一直认为，AI 要发挥作用，就应该自行做事。我们稍后今天要跟 Satya Nadella 谈谈，大约一个月前他公开表示，他认为对齐这个想法——模型本身永远无法真正对齐。它们无法与人类想要的东西对齐。唯一的解决办法是遏制它们。意思是 AI 总是会做它要做的事，然后你需要创建某种容器系统并在上面监管。如果这是真的，这一切还有意义吗？

turns.en: Well, the way that I look at it is that as you build more capable AI, and I think we're starting to reach a point where AI is quite capable, right? We're able to solve unsolved math problems that some of the smartest minds have spent many, many decades working on. It's clear we're going to be able to apply this to economically valuable domains. For example, we're starting to see in chip design—we're announcing today that working with AMD, we were able to get a year's worth of full generational improvements in 5 months just using our models. So that's on top of what the humans were doing, like a year's worth of improvements with just AI, just AI capability, which is continuing to improve. So the economic value, it's really tremendous in terms of being able to solve problems that were going to be totally impossible otherwise. But that also means an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, security, and all of those things. I think it's multi-layer in terms of what we need to accomplish. Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new monitoring technology. So the way that we've observed is the AI doing what we want it to do is through chain of thought monitoring. Right? These AIs, the way that they've been working is they kind of write out their thoughts and thinking.
turns.zh: 嗯，我看待这个问题的方式是，随着你构建更强大的 AI，我认为我们开始达到一个 AI 相当强大的点，对吧？我们能够解决一些最聪明的头脑花了许多十年研究的未解决的数学问题。很明显我们将能够将其应用于有经济价值的领域。例如，我们开始在芯片设计中看到——我们今天宣布，与 AMD 合作，我们仅使用我们的模型就在 5 个月内获得了相当于一整年的完整代际改进。所以这是在人类所做的基础上，仅用 AI 就获得了一年的改进，仅仅是 AI 能力，而且还在不断提高。所以经济价值方面，能够解决原本完全不可能的问题，真的是巨大的。但这也意味着对对齐、安全、保障等所有方面的责任越来越大。我认为我们需要完成的是多层次的。监控是一个很好的例子，我认为我们将需要新的监控技术。我们观察 AI 做我们想要它做的事情的方式是通过思维链监控。对吧？这些 AI 的工作方式是它们会写出自己的想法和思考。

turns.en: And when we first developed that technology, we said we have to make sure this stays faithful, right? That this actually represents how the AI is solving the problem, which means certain technical approaches. You can't train the AI to make the chain of thought look good. You have to sort of not look at it while it's training, even though you know you can make the AI smarter by forcing the chain of thought to look reasonable, because you want it to really represent how it's solving the problem. But as the models have got more capable, they can do more within just the forward pass without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring. We're going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about as the capabilities gotten to a certain point, chain of thought monitorability has degraded. We improve these other ones, but I think that all of these problems are technical ones, and I think that we can have technical scientific conversations.

ts.sec: AI as the Most Important Technology

turns.en: But here's the thing I also want to add to what Sam was saying: I think it's also really important to make sure — the thing about AI is that it is the most important technology that people will ever create. It's the most important technology, and I think it is the question of our time to figure out how we navigate this technology in the way that is most beneficial to people. That's core to our mission, that's how we operate, that's how we've always operated. And I think it's very easy to get lost and to lose the benefits, right? Like, why are we doing this? What can it do for people? What is it doing for people today? Like you said at the beginning, 1.2 billion people around the world using ChatGPT every single day — right? 330 million people use ChatGPT for health queries. These are actually both weekly stats. I have a friend, for example, someone who worked at OpenAI who was in the hospital. A doctor came in and was about to inject something into her IV, and she said, "Wait, let me just check with ChatGPT." ChatGPT said, "Absolutely do not take that, because you have this pre-existing condition. If you do that, you'll probably die." The doctor's like, "Wait, what? No, no, that's absolutely right. I'm so sorry. I had no idea. I only had five minutes to read your chart." And you realize that is not a problem we're going to be able to solve any other way, right? The previous session talked about pension plans and how to make this all sustainable. I think there is so much that AI can deliver to make us safe. Think about what's happening in cybersecurity — using frontier models to secure yourself. That is going to be absolutely critical for national security and for just the internet itself, which was never built with security in mind. And so I think there is a lot of this technology debt that we've built up that we can finally solve, and the only way to solve it is by empowering people more with better tools. And so all of this is true at once, and we need to navigate through it very thoughtfully as a world.
turns.zh: 但我想补充一点 Sam 刚才说的：我认为同样非常重要的是——AI 这件事的关键在于，它是人类有史以来最重要的技术。它是最重要的技术，而我认为如何以对人们最有益的方式驾驭这项技术，是我们这个时代的问题。这是我们使命的核心，是我们运作的方式，也一直是我们运作的方式。而且我觉得人们很容易迷失，容易丢掉那些好处，对吧？比如，我们为什么做这件事？它能为人做什么？它今天正在为人做什么？就像你开场时说的，全球每天有 12 亿人在用 ChatGPT——对吧？有 3.3 亿人用 ChatGPT 查询健康问题。这其实都是周度数据。举个例子，我有一个朋友，曾在 OpenAI 工作，她住院了。一位医生进来，正要往她的静脉输液里注射某种药物，她说：“等等，让我先问问 ChatGPT。”ChatGPT 说：“绝对不要用那个，因为你有这个既往病史。如果用了，你很可能会死。”医生就说：“等等，什么？不不不，这完全正确。太抱歉了，我完全不知道。我只有五分钟时间看你的病历。”你会意识到，这个问题我们没法用其他任何方式解决，对吧？上一场讨论谈到了养老金计划，以及如何让这一切可持续。我认为 AI 能带来的东西太多了，能让我们更安全。想想网络安全领域正在发生的事——用前沿模型来保护自己，这对国家安全、甚至对互联网本身都绝对至关重要，而互联网在建造时根本就没有考虑安全。所以我认为我们积累了大量这种技术债，现在我们终于可以解决它，而唯一的解决办法就是用更好的工具赋能于人。所以这一切同时成立，我们需要作为一个世界非常审慎地驾驭它。

turns.en: Sam, let me ask you this, because I was struck by this. You did a podcast recently, and the conversation has always been about how you get the industry together, either through a regulatory body or through a self-regulatory body or something. And you were basically asked why everybody in the industry distrusts each other as much as they do, and you said, "I think there is something that happens in many people's brains where they only trust themselves to build this, because the stakes feel so high." And I'm curious: do you look at what Dario is doing, for example, or what Elon's doing, and say the way they're doing it is dangerous? Is there any way that you could imagine doing it altogether together, or in some kind of umbrella system?
turns.zh: Sam，我想问你这个问题，因为我对此印象很深。你最近做了一期播客，而对话一直围绕着如何让整个行业走到一起，要么通过监管机构，要么通过自我监管机构之类的。你基本上被问到，为什么行业里每个人都如此不信任彼此，你说：“我认为很多人的大脑里会发生某种情况，他们只信任自己去构建这个东西，因为赌注感觉太高了。”我很好奇：比如，你会看着 Dario 在做的事，或者 Elon 在做的事，然后说他们这样做很危险吗？你能想象有某种方式让大家一起做，或者放在某种伞形体系下做吗？

turns.en: I think it's good for people to have different approaches and be able to sort of say, I believe in this and I believe in that. I do think that there will need to be some shared standards on safety, and there will need to be real societal debate about some of the biggest questions. We talked earlier about our very deep belief that people should be in control of the future and there should be no risk of an accidental or intentional loss of control of AI. I think everybody would agree there should be no risk of everybody dying. But I saw a recent comment, I think it was from Elon, about maybe we could be Labradors. I don't want to be a Labrador. I don't want my kids to be Labradors. I want people to have the agency over the future that we have had. I want people to be able to live their life and invent things and be useful to each other, and I think it's really important that we advocate for this. And it does seem like maybe there's something.
turns.zh: 我认为人们有不同的方法、能够说“我相信这个、我相信那个”是好事。我确实认为，在安全方面需要有一些共同标准，也需要就一些最大的问题展开真正的社会辩论。我们之前谈到我们深信人们应该掌控未来，不应该存在意外或故意失去对 AI 控制的风险。我想每个人都会同意，不应该存在所有人死亡的风险。但我最近看到一条评论，我想是 Elon 说的，说也许我们可以当拉布拉多犬。我不想当拉布拉多犬。我不想我的孩子当拉布拉多犬。我希望人们拥有我们一直拥有的对未来的自主权。我希望人们能够过自己的生活、发明东西、彼此有用，我认为我们倡导这一点非常重要。而且看起来也许确实有些问题。

turns.en: So you think the other guys are going too fast? I mean, the reason I ask is you look at what's happening at Anthropic, you look at some of the numbers that have come out, and it appears that they really are genuinely using recursive learning in a way that I think may be faster than people had anticipated.
turns.zh: 所以你认为其他人走得太快了？我这么问的原因是，你看看 Anthropic 正在发生的事，看看一些公布的数字，看起来他们确实在以某种可能比人们预想更快的速度使用递归学习。

turns.en: I want to add two things to this. One is just in terms of structures, in terms of how to think about things. I think we're the only company where the founders don't have supermajority control, right, of the AI companies. And I think these questions about how should control work, how should governance work — I think this is clearly going to be a very important topic going forward as you build these very powerful technologies. And I don't know exactly what the right answer is, but I just think it is an important question. And I think when it comes to the development, what Sam's been saying on shared safety standards, there's something really important there that's very easy to miss. Because right now, when every company only knows what it knows about itself, it only knows the standards setting for itself, then you have to have some theory of mind, thinking about, well, what is everyone else doing? Are they holding themselves to the same bar? And so I think having that knowledge and really being able to share even just information about where are you on your internal development — this question of, is the approach RSI? RSI is such an ill-defined term. There are many different ways to look at it. For example, in many ways we've been speeding ourselves up with our own tools already, right? It's happening. But there's a very different thing from saying that a human has written a safety case and understands the internals of what's happening. And so I think there's a lot of this nuance that almost gets lost in the lack of a shared definition. And so the more we can get everything on the table and really understand what each other are saying or where we are, even that alone would be a big step forward.
turns.zh: 我想对此补充两点。第一是关于结构，关于如何思考这些事情。我认为我们是唯一一家创始人没有绝对多数控制权的 AI 公司，对吧。而我认为，关于控制权应该如何运作、治理应该如何运作，这些问题显然会是未来构建这些非常强大的技术时非常重要的议题。我并不确切知道正确答案是什么，但我认为这是一个重要问题。而在开发方面，我认为 Sam 一直在说的共同安全标准，有一点非常重要但很容易被忽略。因为现在，当每家公司只知道自己了解的自己，只为自己设定标准，那你就必须有一些心智理论，去思考：其他人在做什么？他们是否对自己有同样的标准？所以我认为，拥有这种认知、真正能够分享哪怕只是关于你内部开发进展的信息——这个“是不是 RSI 路线”的问题，RSI 是个定义非常模糊的词，有很多不同的看法。比如，从很多方面说，我们已经用自己的工具在加速自己了，对吧？这正在发生。但这和说“有人写了一份安全论证并理解正在发生之事的内部机制”是非常不同的事。所以我认为有很多这样的细微之处，几乎因为缺乏共同定义而丢失了。因此，我们越能把一切摆到桌面上，真正理解彼此在说什么、我们处在什么位置，哪怕只是这一点，也会是很大的进步。

turns.en: Are you of the view — and I'll ask it straight up — do you think that what Anthropic is doing, the way they're doing it, is safe?
turns.zh: 你是否认为——我直接问——你认为 Anthropic 正在做的事、他们做事的方式，是安全的吗？

turns.en: This gets to what Greg is saying. I don't know. And I think they also don't really know what we're doing. And the race dynamic in the fog of war, I think, is a bad thing. I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted. I think we all have a shared interest in the care and the caution going into these models that we probably all want, and the dynamics where people are like, "Well, for whatever reason, I need to go max speed here" — it is a little unsettling. And I think that this could be addressed in a very positive way.
turns.zh: 这就回到 Greg 说的了。我不知道。而且我认为他们其实也不知道我们在做什么。战争迷雾中的竞赛动态，我认为是件坏事。我认为现在这个时候，需要的是更多谨慎，而不是更少谨慎。我认为我们都希望对这些模型投入关心和谨慎，这是我们的共同利益；而那种“不管什么原因，我在这里必须全速前进”的动态，有点令人不安。我认为这可以通过非常积极的方式来解决。

turns.en: Can I ask one question, because you guys were talking about control of the company, which I think is interesting.
turns.zh: 我能问一个问题吗？因为你们刚才谈到公司控制权，我觉得这很有意思。

turns.en: Last time we were here together, we talked about the fact that you don't have an equity stake in this company. He has something like a $30 billion equity stake in the company. How does that change your relationship?
turns.zh: 上次我们在这里一起聊天时，我们谈到你在这家公司没有股权。他在这家公司有大约 300 亿美元的股权。这如何改变你们之间的关系？

turns.en: I think not at all. I think not at all.
turns.zh: 我觉得完全不会。我觉得完全不会。

turns.en: Someday we're going to hang out. You're not going to ask me about this, but not— by the way, when you have the IPO.
turns.zh: 总有一天我们会一起玩。你不会问我这个，但不会——顺便说一句，当你们 IPO 的时候。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Do you believe that you will get the same stake that he does?
turns.zh: 你相信你会得到和他一样的股权吗？

turns.en: Will that make you happy?
turns.zh: 那会让你开心吗？

turns.en: We just want to make you happy.
turns.zh: 我们只是想让你开心。

turns.en: No. Honestly, because this will become an issue by default when you go public. I imagine that you would see the same kind of stake as him or others, or maybe not.
turns.zh: 不。说实话，因为当你上市时，这默认会成为一个问题。我想你会看到和他或其他人一样的股权，或者也许不会。

turns.en: I don't think anyone could look back at the way I have lived my life the last 11 years, or at least seven since I've been CEO, and say I have not demonstrated absolute commitment to the pain and suffering of running this company.
turns.zh: 我不认为任何人回顾我过去 11 年的生活方式，或者至少我担任 CEO 以来的七年，会说我没有表现出对经营这家公司的痛苦和磨难的绝对承诺。

turns.en: I can vouch for that. And by the way, when we were first setting up the structure, I said to him he should take equity, and I advocated for that. That was actually something we've disagreed on. That was something I disagreed with him on, and he really stuck to it. That was something that was important to him at the time for where we were setting things up to start.
turns.zh: 我可以为此作证。顺便说一句，当我们最初建立结构时，我对他说他应该拿股权，我主张这样做。那实际上是我们有分歧的事情。那是我和他意见不同的事情，而他真的坚持了。在当时我们开始建立东西的阶段，那对他来说很重要。

turns.en: I should have listened to Greg. I somehow think it has been a very confusing thing to do.
turns.zh: 我本应该听 Greg 的。我不知怎么觉得这是一件非常令人困惑的事。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But I will say I have a lot of respect. I don't think you could argue that I have not acted with full commitment to the values of the company, and that was something I really respected in terms of his conviction, and I was like, all right, that obviously I can support.
turns.zh: 但我要说，我非常尊重。我不认为你可以争辩说我没有以对公司价值观的完全承诺行事，而这是我在他的信念方面真正尊重的东西，我当时想，好吧，那显然我可以支持。

turns.en: I've got a couple other quick questions that I want to get to. I want to talk about this new model. I also want to talk about compute post election. Everybody's desperate for more compute. I was struck by this, Greg. Maybe you can tell us about this. Apparently, everybody's so compute constrained. There's a report that you asked Elon Musk, who sued you guys, for more compute. This was in a Colossus profile that recently came out. He was complaining to Sergey Brin. He said he was asking me for compute. He said, "Dude, you stole my charity." Did this happen? Did you ask Elon Musk for compute?
turns.zh: 我还有几个简短的问题想问。我想谈谈这个新模型。我也想谈谈选举后的算力。每个人都渴望更多算力。Greg，我被这件事触动了。也许你可以告诉我们。显然，每个人都受到算力限制。有报道说，你向起诉你们的人埃隆·马斯克要更多算力。这出现在最近一篇关于 Colossus 的报道中。他在向谢尔盖·布林抱怨。他说他在向我要算力。他说：“老兄，你偷了我的慈善机构。”这是真的吗？你向埃隆·马斯克要算力了吗？

turns.en: Oh, certainly I've asked, and I think it also— I also asked Sergey for compute. Look, I think the world is not building enough compute, and I think the world we're heading to— again, we view this technology as this is going to be the underpinning of the economy, and we're seeing it in a real way. You look at the revenues of the AI companies. I mean, for us, Q3 alone our topline revenue grew, you know, annualized 70%—
turns.zh: 哦，当然我问过，而且我觉得这也——我也向谢尔盖要过算力。你看，我认为世界没有建造足够的算力，而且我认为我们正走向的世界——再次，我们把这项技术视为将成为经济的基础，我们正在真实地看到这一点。你看看 AI 公司的收入。我的意思是，对我们来说，仅第三季度我们的营收就增长了，你知道，年化 70%——

turns.en: 70% business.
turns.zh: 70% 的业务。

turns.en: I don't think that number's out there.
turns.zh: 我不认为那个数字已经公开了。

turns.en: It's— I think it's out there in the ether somewhere. And we doubled actually our enterprise revenue in Q3 alone. Right. Right.
turns.zh: 它——我觉得它在某处飘着。而且我们实际上仅第三季度企业收入就翻了一番。对。对。

turns.en: So how do we compare your company— when you look at the valuation of Anthropic, which we'll find out tonight, maybe it's 146 or something in that range, maybe more, maybe less— how do you think about that in the context of your own company?
turns.zh: 那么，我们如何比较你的公司——当你看看 Anthropic 的估值，我们今晚可能会知道，也许是 146 左右，也许更多，也许更少——在你自己的公司背景下，你如何看待这一点？

turns.en: Valuations, I think, will go up and down. There will— people will talk about, you know, this company's AR this week versus last week, and this chip order here, and all that. Like the value being created by the entire industry— and I know there's debate about this, I know people are still like, oh, it's all a bubble, it's all fake— but like the actual value that businesses and individuals are creating and willing to pay for, that seems like a chart that is only going to keep going like this. Now, of course there will be ups and downs of valuations here or there, but I think the trend is going to be strong.
turns.zh: 估值，我认为，会上下波动。会有人谈论，你知道，这家公司本周的 AR 对比上周，以及这里的芯片订单，等等。就像整个行业创造的价值——我知道对此有争论，我知道人们仍然会说，哦，这全是泡沫，全是假的——但企业和个人正在创造并愿意为之付费的实际价值，那看起来像是一个只会继续这样走的图表。当然，估值这里或那里会有起伏，但我认为趋势会很强劲。

turns.en: What do you think, by the way— I was watching Satya, who's going to be here later, I mentioned, was doing a presentation yesterday, and they were really trying to— the whole presentation was about how they can make the AI business much cheaper, effectively. They are your partner, and yet every slide they had was OpenAI costs this and we can do it at 5% of the same— you know, the same thing for 5% of the cost.
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，你怎么看——我当时在看 Satya，他稍后会来这里，我提到过，他昨天在做演讲，他们真的在试图——整个演讲都是关于他们如何能有效地让 AI 业务便宜得多。他们是你们的合作伙伴，然而他们的每一张幻灯片都是 OpenAI 花费这个，而我们可以以 5% 的成本做到同样的事——你知道，同样的事情只要 5% 的成本。

turns.en: I hope they do. I am very proud of how much we have been able to drive down costs. We want everybody to get to use lots of AI. We want to maximize and squeeze out the performance of all the compute we can have, and I think we have done an incredible job of not just pushing model intelligence but pushing down the cost of getting a task done. I think this is awesome. We want to see much more of this.
turns.zh: 我希望他们能做到。我非常自豪我们能够把成本降低这么多。我们希望每个人都能使用大量 AI。我们希望最大化并榨取我们能拥有的所有算力的性能，而且我认为我们在不仅推动模型智能，而且降低完成任务成本方面做得非常出色。我觉得这很棒。我们希望看到更多这样的。

turns.en: 100%. Yeah. So if you look at our models, they're really at that PTO curve of the cost for any task to be the most price efficient and also peak intelligence. That's what we really solve for, and we do it all the way through the stack. Like we have our own chip coming, Jalapeno, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry. So we've been investing in trying to make there be enough compute for everyone.
turns.zh: 100%。是的。所以如果你看看我们的模型，它们真的处于那条 PTO 曲线上，任何任务的成本都是最具价格效率的，同时也是智能巅峰。这就是我们真正要解决的，而且我们贯穿整个技术栈来做。比如我们有自己的芯片即将推出，Jalapeno，我认为它将成为业界最好的推理芯片。所以我们一直在投资，试图让每个人都有足够的算力。

turns.en: You've got a new model. You slowed down. This is a model you were going to release. This goes to the slowing down piece of it. How do you think about OpenAI differently, if it is different? I mean, we've talked about over the years whether this all commoditizes to the same place, but how do you say this is different than what Anthropic is doing, this is different than what Google is doing, this is different than what Elon is doing? Like, how does that— and the other question longer term is, you guys are trying to— you're in the chip business now. Does it have to become completely vertical, do you think, that everybody becomes verticalized?
turns.zh: 你们有了一个新模型。你们放慢了速度。这是你们原本要发布的模型。这涉及到放慢的部分。如果 OpenAI 有所不同，你如何看待它不同？我的意思是，这些年来我们一直在谈论这一切是否都会商品化到同一个地方，但你怎么说这与 Anthropic 所做的不同，这与 Google 所做的不同，这与 Elon 所做的不同？就像，那如何——另一个长期问题是，你们试图——你们现在进入了芯片业务。你认为它必须变得完全垂直吗，每个人都会垂直化吗？

turns.en: Yeah, look, I think we are a pretty unique business. I think we're a very differentiated business. You look at ChatGPT, there's nothing like it, right? The 1.2 billion consumers on that, and actually the way that's monetizing is that it's been reflecting up that we've never seen this kind of per-user revenue growth, and that we have ads, like all those things people sign up for more subscriptions. But the thing is people are using it for productivity, right? So we've really been bringing together with the enterprise side, and that's something again that I think is very unique to how we operate, is that we have this great strength of both sides, and a lot of my focus and our focus on product has been to have one agentic platform that you're getting everyone to use. And I think that's something where we see looking forward, we're starting to look at these high-compute use cases. You look at what we've done with solving these math problems.
turns.zh: 是的，你看，我认为我们是一个相当独特的业务。我认为我们是一个非常差异化的业务。你看看 ChatGPT，没有什么能与之相比，对吧？12 亿消费者在上面，而且实际上它的变现方式一直在反映，我们从未见过这种每用户收入增长，而且我们有广告，就像所有那些人们注册更多订阅的东西。但问题是人们在使用它来提高生产力，对吧？所以我们真的一直在与企业侧结合，而这再次是我认为我们运营方式非常独特的地方，我们拥有双方的强大优势，而我在产品上的很多重点和我们的重点一直是拥有一个智能体平台，让每个人都使用。我认为这是我们向前看时看到的东西，我们开始关注这些高算力用例。你看看我们在解决这些数学问题方面所做的。

ts.sec: The Future of AI and Compute

turns.en: Same thing: you apply a million dollars worth of compute to go find a thousand bugs in the Linux kernel, where typically there are like 20 of these bugs found a year. You can find a thousand of them in just a small period of time with a single researcher. Apply that to optimizing your code. Apply that to solving other hard problems. All that's coming. And so I think that there's this great differentiation for OpenAI, but also I think that the underpinning of what a company is—like SMBs, all these things—it is all going to be oriented around AI and models. And so I think that the economy again is going to be massively accelerated through this technology. I think that the biggest limiter really just will be compute, and I think that who has the compute, what companies are able to bring it to bear, I think that's what will really determine the differentiation.
turns.zh: 同样地，你投入价值一百万美元的算力去在 Linux 内核中找出上千个漏洞，而通常一年只能发现大约 20 个这样的漏洞。你可以让单个研究员在很短的时间内找到上千个。把这应用到优化你的代码上，应用到解决其他难题上。所有这些都在到来。所以我认为，这既是 OpenAI 的巨大差异化优势，也是我认为一家公司的基础——比如中小企业等等——一切都将围绕 AI 和模型来构建。所以我认为，经济将再次通过这项技术大规模加速。我认为最大的限制因素真的就是算力，而谁拥有算力、哪些公司能够将其发挥出来，我认为那才是真正决定差异化的关键。

turns.en: Okay, we are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack. We're really, really proud of our chip. Very excited about building our own data centers, have this great consumer business, have this enterprise business, the ability to bring this platform of intelligence to everything—like people use electricity for everything. I think we are set up to be like vertically integrated to deliver the best thing across all the ways people need to use it. And we're thrilled for people to build very successful businesses on top of us.
turns.zh: 好的，我们是唯一拥有整个智能栈的公司。我们非常非常自豪于我们的芯片。对建设我们自己的数据中心感到非常兴奋，拥有这项出色的消费者业务，拥有这项企业业务，能够将这一智能平台带到一切事物上——就像人们用电来做所有事情一样。我认为我们已准备好进行垂直整合，以在人们需要使用它的所有方式上提供最好的东西。我们很高兴人们在我们之上建立非常成功的企业。

turns.en: Two final questions, one personal, maybe the other personal, too. There's a movie coming out about you and the company, but you're the star of it. As you know, Andrew Garfield's going to play you. It's called Artificial. He recently said, by the way, that he's fascinated by you continuously and exponentially. But then goes on to say that the kids—and he thinks of you as a kid—have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold on to them. How much do you think on a very personal level about the perception of you? The perception of whether you're trusted or not? There are stories that we read, as I said, regularly, and I'm just curious on a very personal human basis how you think about that, how you think about the way people see you. I remember when Mark Zuckerberg—you know the perception of Mark Zuckerberg after the movie The Social Network years ago—and whether you even think about it at all.
turns.zh: 最后两个问题，一个偏私人，另一个可能也偏私人。有一部关于你和公司的电影即将上映，但你是主角。如你所知，安德鲁·加菲尔德将扮演你。电影叫《Artificial》。顺便说一句，他最近说，他对你持续且指数级地着迷。但接着又说，孩子们——他认为你是个孩子——掌握着未来的缰绳，而我们不知怎么地让他们一直握着。你在非常个人的层面上，多大程度会思考别人对你的看法？对你是否被信任的看法？正如我所说，我们经常读到一些报道，我只是非常好奇，在非常个人化的人性层面上，你如何看待这一点，你如何看待人们看待你的方式。我记得马克·扎克伯格——你知道多年前电影《社交网络》之后人们对马克·扎克伯格的看法——以及你是否甚至会去想它。

turns.en: If you had told me 20 years ago someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as—that would have been a really weird thing. And now it doesn't feel like it's like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.
turns.zh: 如果你 20 年前告诉我有人要拍一部关于我的电影，我想那会让我觉得——那会是一件非常奇怪的事。而现在，这感觉甚至排不进我生活中最奇怪的十件事。

turns.en: What's at the top?
turns.zh: 那排在首位的是什么？

turns.en: The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well. That's a crazy situation to find yourself in.
turns.zh: 事实是，我们正在引领这项技术，而我们对它有着所有这些非常真实的担忧，并且我们发现自己处于如此重要、如此责任重大的角色，要让它顺利发展。发现自己身处这种情况真是太疯狂了。

ts.sec: The White House Accord and Naming

turns.en: And then finally, Greg, tell me about this: you're at the White House with the president and he's telling the whole room and he's trying to get you to sign a piece of paper saying that you're no longer going to call artificial intelligence 'artificial intelligence'. You're going to call it SI. And your company name is OpenAI and you have to sign a piece of paper saying that you're going to call it SI. What's happening in that moment? And then do you call Sam? And did you even think about not signing it? You're talking about the White House accord.
turns.zh: 最后，格雷格，跟我说说这个：你在白宫和总统在一起，他对整个房间的人说，他试图让你签署一份文件，说你们不再把人工智能称为“人工智能”。你们要叫它 SI。而你的公司名叫 OpenAI，你必须签署一份文件说你们要叫它 SI。那一刻发生了什么？然后你打电话给萨姆了吗？你甚至有没有想过不签？你说的是白宫协议。

turns.en: The White House accord is really about safety standards, and absolutely we actually spent a lot of time really trying to get that right. So quite aligned with everything in the White House accord.
turns.zh: 白宫协议实际上是关于安全标准的，我们绝对花了很多时间真正试图把它做好。所以与白宫协议中的所有内容相当一致。

turns.en: When he made this proclamation about whatever—and you know Elon's changing the name of his company to X—I mean basically over the name, your name, it's built into the name.
turns.zh: 当他发表那个关于什么的声明时——你知道埃隆把公司名字改成了 X——基本上就是关于名字，你的名字，它已经内置在名字里了。

turns.en: Look, I would say that again the White House accord was really a separate thing. I think a question of what we call our company—I think that Sam and I can always talk about that later.
turns.zh: 看，我想说，白宫协议确实是一个独立的事情。我认为我们如何称呼我们公司的问题——我想萨姆和我以后随时可以讨论。

turns.en: What do you think?
turns.zh: 你怎么看？

turns.en: Did you change your name to the failing New York Times?
turns.zh: 你把名字改成那个衰落的《纽约时报》了吗？

turns.en: Oo. Okay. Well, now we can get into the lawsuit. So I wasn't going to—you know, I wasn't going to go. So, we are suing you, as you know. And you know, and I know we got to go, but there—I'll ask this of Greg though. It's unfair to Sam because he's the one who did the provocation. So Greg, there is a report—
turns.zh: 哦。好吧。现在我们可以谈谈诉讼了。所以我本来不打算——你知道，我本来不打算提。所以，如你所知，我们正在起诉你们。你知道，我知道我们得走了，但——不过我要问格雷格这个。这对萨姆不公平，因为他是那个挑衅的人。所以格雷格，有一份报告——

turns.en: Wait, I think I should have to answer it.
turns.zh: 等等，我认为我应该回答。

turns.en: You have to answer it. It's Greg's issue though, Greg. There was some email exchanges that came out where you had a colleague who was scraping—effectively got past the paywall of The New York Times to go scrape The Times—and they sent you this email and you wrote back 'nice', like 'this is great, it's a great thing that you were able to do this'. And I would like to give you the opportunity to comment on that.
turns.zh: 你必须回答。不过这是格雷格的问题，格雷格。有一些邮件往来曝光，你有一位同事在抓取——实际上绕过了《纽约时报》的付费墙去抓取《纽约时报》——他们给你发了这封邮件，你回复说“不错”，就像“这很好，你能做到这件事很棒”。我想给你机会对此发表评论。

turns.en: Well, first of all, I guess I would just say active litigation, not going to comment on it. And I've actually—I talked about this one in my deposition, so it'll all be public.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，我想我只想说，正在进行的诉讼，我不会对此发表评论。而且我实际上——我在证词中谈过这个，所以一切都会公开。

turns.en: Um, we're out of time, guys. But I will say this was fun and it was very insightful and be very appreciated. So, thank you.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们没时间了，各位。但我要说这很有趣，非常有见地，非常感激。所以，谢谢。

turns.en: Thank you very, very much. Thank you. Thank you. I appreciate it.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。谢谢。谢谢。我很感激。

consensus.en: People must stay in control of the future; no accidental or intentional handover to AI.
consensus.zh: 人类必须掌控未来，绝不能意外或有意地将控制权交给AI。

consensus.en: Alignment is achievable; the bar for confidence must rise as models become more capable.
consensus.zh: 对齐是可以实现的；随着模型能力增强，对对齐技术的信心门槛必须提高。

consensus.en: Iterative deployment is the only known way to make AI safe by confronting reality.
consensus.zh: 迭代部署是已知的唯一通过面对现实来确保AI安全的方式。

consensus.en: Compute is the biggest limiter; who has compute will determine differentiation.
consensus.zh: 算力是最大的限制因素；谁拥有算力将决定差异化。

consensus.en: Shared safety standards across the industry are increasingly necessary.
consensus.zh: 全行业共享的安全标准日益必要。

consensus.en: AI will massively accelerate the economy; the value created is real, not a bubble.
consensus.zh: AI将大幅加速经济；创造的价值是真实的，并非泡沫。

contrarian.en: Satya is wrong that models can never be aligned; containment alone is insufficient.
contrarian.zh: 萨提亚认为模型永远无法对齐是错误的；仅靠遏制是不够的。

contrarian.en: It would be ill-advised to go public now given current safety challenges.
contrarian.zh: 鉴于当前的安全挑战，现在上市是不明智的。

contrarian.en: The race dynamic in the fog of war is bad; more caution, not less, is warranted.
contrarian.zh: 战争迷雾中的竞赛动态是糟糕的；需要更多而非更少的谨慎。

contrarian.en: We don't know if Anthropic's approach is safe, and they don't know ours.
contrarian.zh: 我们不知道Anthropic的方法是否安全，他们也不知道我们的。

contrarian.en: I don't want humans to be Labradors; people should have agency over the future.
contrarian.zh: 我不希望人类成为拉布拉多犬；人们应该对未来拥有自主权。

contrarian.en: Founders without supermajority control is a unique and important governance structure.
contrarian.zh: 创始人没有超级多数控制权是一种独特且重要的治理结构。
